claim: The IQGAP family of proteins plays a key role in actin cytoskeleton regulation including the assembly and function of the contractile actomyosin ring in budding and fission yeasts.
source: The IQGAP family of proteins plays a key role in actin cytoskeleton regulation including the assembly and function of the contractile actomyosin ring in budding and fission yeasts (Briggs and Sacks, 2003; Eng et al., 1998; Epp and Chant, 1997; Lippincott and Li, 1998; Tebbs and Pollard, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: During cytokinesis, Rng2 is tethered to the plasma membrane via Mid1, ensuring the formation and anchoring of the cytokinetic ring.
source: We chose this approach, since during cytokinesis Rng2, which binds several actomyosin ring proteins, is tethered to the plasma membrane via Mid1, ensuring the formation and anchoring of the cytokinetic ring (Laplante et al., 2016; Laporte et al., 2011; Padmanabhan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Actin filaments landing onto His6-Rng2(1-189) decorated SLBs formed highly bent arcs and full rings with curvatures of Ccurly = 1.7 ± 0.5 µm−1.
source: Remarkably, actin filaments landing onto His6-Rng2(1-189) decorated SLBs formed highly bent arcs and full rings with curvatures of Ccurly = 1.7 ± 0.5 µm−1 (Figure 1B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in figures and videos showing measured curvatures.

claim: Binding of membrane tethering actin binding proteins such as the CHD of α-actinin or the actin binding domain of Ezrin did not appreciably bend actin filaments.
source: Binding of other membrane tethering actin binding proteins in the same geometry, such as the CHD of α-actinin or the actin binding domain of Ezrin, did not appreciably bend actin filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Membrane anchored fimbrin has been shown not to bend actin.
source: Membrane anchored fimbrin has also been shown not to bend actin (Murrell and Gardel, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The bending of individual actin filaments into rings by His6-Rng2(1-189) is an unprecedented phenomenon among known actin binding proteins.
source: To our knowledge, the bending of individual actin filaments into rings is an unprecedented phenomenon among the known actin binding proteins and we will refer in the following to His6-Rng2(1-189) as 'curly'.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the field and comparison with known actin binding proteins.

claim: Curly mobility within planar lipid membranes is important for actin bending.
source: Curly mobility within planar lipid membranes was important for actin bending as glass adsorbed, immobilized His6-Curly led to reduced actin binding and bending (Cglass = 0.6 ± 0.3 µm−1) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing mobile versus immobilized curly.

claim: Placing the hexa-histidine tag to the C-terminus (Rng2(1-189)-His6) did not affect actin filament bending (Ccurly-his = 1.5 ± 0.5 µm−1).
source: However, placing the hexa-histidine tag to the C-terminus, Rng2(1-189)-His6, did not affect actin filament bending (Ccurly-his = 1.5 ± 0.5 µm−1) (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing similar curvatures with C-terminal tag.

claim: The bending of actin filaments by curly was oriented anti-clockwise with respect to the plus end in all instances where the plus end was clearly labeled.
source: We found that the bending was oriented anti-clockwise with respect to the plus end in all instances, wherein the plus end was clearly labeled to identify the orientation of filament bending (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using labeled capping protein to mark the plus end.

claim: The internal sequence of the two actin binding sites within curly sets the chirality of actin bending and not the position of the membrane linker.
source: This was observed using both, the N-terminal and C-terminal hexa-histidine tagged curly, indicating that the internal sequence of the two actin binding sites within curly sets the chirality of actin bending and not the position of the membrane linker (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing consistent bending orientation regardless of tag position.

claim: Actin filaments appeared to bend concomitant with their landing on the supported lipid bilayer.
source: Actin filaments appeared to bend concomitant with their landing on the supported lipid bilayer, which indicates that the bending did not require the full actin filament to be tethered to the SLB and underlined the earlier observation that the bending occurred locally.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from experimental data and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Actin filaments polymerized by membrane tethered formin in the presence of membrane tethered His6-Curly displayed characteristic bending shortly after the onset of polymerization (Cformin, short = 1.1 ± 0.3 µm−1) and often grew into full rings (Cformin rings = 1.7 ± 0.4 µm−1).
source: Strikingly, actin filaments displayed characteristic bending shortly after the onset of polymerization (Cformin, short = 1.1 ± 0.3 µm−1) and often grew into full rings (Cformin rings = 1.7 ± 0.4 µm−1) (Figure 3C,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E; Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing curvature measurements during formin-driven polymerization.

claim: Polymerization of actin filaments along SLBs decorated with His10-SNAP-EzrinABD did not result in the formation of arcs or rings.
source: By contrast, polymerization of actin filaments along SLBs decorated with His10-SNAP-EzrinABD did not result in the formation of arcs or rings, establishing that actin filament bending was due to curly and not due to formin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experimental data showing no bending with EzrinABD.

claim: Actin bending occurs continuously due to the binding of membrane tethered curly and did not require the cross-linking of adjacent ends of the same filament.
source: These observations show that actin bending occurs continuously due to the binding of membrane tethered curly and did not require the cross-linking of adjacent ends of the same filament as was observed with the actin cross-linker anillin (Kučera et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and comparison with another actin cross-linker.

claim: The binding site of curly with actin filaments defines an orientation with the propagation of an established curved trajectory.
source: Importantly, the uni-directional bending supports the hypothesis that the binding site of curly with actin filaments defines an orientation with the propagation of an established curved trajectory.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by inference from the observed uni-directional bending.

claim: Addition of tropomyosin to actin filaments increased the frequency of actin ring formation without affecting actin filament curvature.
source: Strikingly, addition of tropomyosin to actin filaments increased the frequency of actin ring formation without affecting actin filament curvature, while actin filaments incubated with the actin cross-linker fimbrin displayed reduced bending and ring formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing actin with tropomyosin versus fimbrin.

claim: Actin filaments incubated with the actin cross-linker fimbrin displayed reduced bending and ring formation.
source: Strikingly, addition of tropomyosin to actin filaments increased the frequency of actin ring formation without affecting actin filament curvature, while actin filaments incubated with the actin cross-linker fimbrin displayed reduced bending and ring formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced bending with fimbrin.

claim: The tropomyosin Cdc8 and curly cooperate to enhance actin filament bending and ring formation.
source: Thus, the tropomyosin Cdc8 and curly cooperate to enhance actin filament bending and ring formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental observation that tropomyosin increases ring formation frequency.

claim: Long actin filaments coated with tropomyosin trace consecutive rings around the same center while landing on curly decorated lipid membranes.
source: Interestingly, we could observe that long actin filaments coated with tropomyosin would trace consecutive rings around the same center while landing on curly decorated lipid membranes.
evidence: The claim is based on direct observation from experimental data.

claim: The second ring formed by tropomyosin-coated actin filaments occupied the interior space of the first ring.
source: Subtraction of the image after completion of the first round of actin filament landing into a ring from the image after the second round revealed that the second ring occupied the interior space of the first ring.
evidence: The claim is supported by image analysis showing the spatial relationship between consecutive rings.

claim: Curly can arrange long actin filaments into an inward-oriented spiral.
source: This would suggest that curly can arrange long actin filaments into an inward-oriented spiral.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of consecutive rings.

claim: Addition of rabbit skeletal muscle myosin II filaments and ATP to actin filaments bound to SLB tethered His6-curly led to increased bending, rotation and finally to ring formation and contraction.
source: Shortly after myosin II addition, actin filaments (curved and straight ones) were propelled by myosin action leading to increased bending, rotation and finally to ring formation and contraction (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–D, Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing actin dynamics after myosin II addition.

claim: Most actin rings displayed a counter-clockwise rotation (34/36 cases) after myosin II addition.
source: Interestingly, most actin rings displayed a counter-clockwise rotation (34/36 cases) and a slow contraction speed of 3 ± 2 nm s−1 (Figure 3F; Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experimental observations.

claim: Actin rings displayed a slow contraction speed of 3 ± 2 nm s−1 after myosin II addition.
source: Interestingly, most actin rings displayed a counter-clockwise rotation (34/36 cases) and a slow contraction speed of 3 ± 2 nm s−1 (Figure 3F; Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data.

claim: The density of actin rings was strongly increased after myosin II addition.
source: The density of actin rings was strongly increased after myosin II addition (Figure 3—figure supplement 5E), indicating that actin sliding leads to more recruitment of curly.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased ring density.

claim: Actin sliding leads to more recruitment of curly.
source: The density of actin rings was strongly increased after myosin II addition (Figure 3—figure supplement 5E), indicating that actin sliding leads to more recruitment of curly.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of increased ring density after myosin II addition.

claim: Actin filament rings displayed increased localization of fluorescently labeled curly after addition of myosin II filaments.
source: In line with this, actin filament rings displayed increased localization of fluorescently labeled curly after addition of myosin II filaments (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased curly fluorescence at actin rings.

claim: Actin rings reached very high curvatures (up to 6.3 µm−1) during the contraction process without breaking.
source: Despite reaching very high actin curvatures (up to 6.3 µm−1) no breaking of actin filaments during the contraction process could be observed suggesting that binding of curly reduces the rigidity of actin filaments.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of high curvatures without filament breakage.

claim: Binding of curly reduces the rigidity of actin filaments.
source: Despite reaching very high actin curvatures (up to 6.3 µm−1) no breaking of actin filaments during the contraction process could be observed suggesting that binding of curly reduces the rigidity of actin filaments.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that actin filaments do not break at high curvatures.

claim: The bending of actin filaments by IQGAP proteins Iqg1(1-330) (S. cerevisiae) and IQGAP1(1–678) (H. sapiens) was conserved (CS.C. = 1.1 ± 0.4 µm−1; CH.S. = 1.0 ± 0.2 µm−1).
source: Since Rng2 belongs to the IQGAP protein family, we tested the N-terminal hexa-histidine tagged fragments of the IQGAP proteins Iqg1(1-330) (S. cerevisiae) and IQGAP1(1–678) (H. sapiens) and found that the bending of actin filaments was conserved (CS.C. = 1.1 ± 0.4 µm−1; CH.S. = 1.0 ± 0.2 µm−1) (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing similar curvatures with IQGAP proteins from different organisms.

claim: The crystal structures of H. sapiens IQGAP1(28–190) and S. pombe Rng2(32-190) indicate high similarity between the two.
source: Comparison of the available crystal structures of H. sapiens IQGAP1(28–190) with S. pombe Rng2(32-190) indicates high similarity between the two (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison of crystal structures.

claim: Expression of GFP-tagged curly in mammalian cell lines HEK293T and RPE-1 resulted in striking changes of the actin cortex architecture with the prominent occurrence of curved and ring-shaped actin filaments and bundles with curvatures of CHEK293T = 2.3 ± 0.4 µm−1 and CRPE-1 = 1.9 ± 0.6 µm−1.
source: Finally, to test the effect of curly on the actin cortex in cells, we expressed GFP -tagged curly in the mammalian cell lines HEK293T and RPE-1, which resulted in striking changes of the actin cortex architecture with the prominent occurrence of curved and ring-shaped actin filaments and bundles with curvatures of CHEK293T = 2.3 ± 0.4 µm−1 and CRPE-1 = 1.9 ± 0.6 µm−1 (Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mammalian cell expression studies.

claim: Co-expression of EGFP-Rng2(1-189) with LifeAct-mCherry confirmed that EGFP-Rng2(1-189) bound to actin filaments in cells.
source: Co-expression with LifeAct-mCherry confirmed EGFP-Rng2(1-189) bound to actin filaments in cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data from cell imaging experiments.

claim: Addition of a CaaX domain to tether curly to cellular membranes did not enhance the actin bending effect but located curly mainly to structures resembling the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: To our surprise, addition of a CaaX domain to tether curly to cellular membranes did not enhance the actin bending effect but located curly mainly to structures resembling the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing unexpected localization of CaaX-tagged curly.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing full-length EGFP-IQGAP1 and LifeAct-mCherry showed curved and ring-shaped actin structures inside the cell as well at its surface.
source: To test whether the actin bending effect is conserved in the mammalian full-length protein, we imaged HEK293T cells expressing full-length EGFP-IQGAP1 and LifeAct-mCherry using lattice light sheet microscopy and indeed observed curved and ring-shaped actin structures inside the cell as well at its surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 5; Video 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from lattice light sheet microscopy.

claim: The actin bending capacity is conserved in full-length IQGAP1.
source: These experiments established that curly could instructively reorganize actin filaments into curved structures and rings and that this capacity is conserved in full-length IQGAP1.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental observations with full-length IQGAP1.

claim: The N-terminal CHD of IQGAP proteins induces actin filament bending when tethered to lipid membranes.
source: Our results show that the N-terminal CHD of IQGAP proteins induces actin filament bending when tethered to lipid membranes, which constitutes a new type of actin binding protein and could be an important link between actin and membrane geometries (for a summary of results, see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all experimental results presented.

claim: This mechanism of actin ring formation stands out as it bends single actin filaments in contrast to other reported systems that generate rings made of bundles of actin filaments.
source: This mechanism of actin ring formation stands out as it bends single actin filaments in contrast to other reported systems that generate rings made of bundles of actin filaments (Litschel et al., 2020; Mavrakis et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2013; Miyazaki et al., 2015; Way et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with other systems cited in the literature.

claim: The actin-binding affinity of Rng2(1-189) is Kd = 0.9 μM.
source: The actin-binding affinity of Rng2(1-189) is Kd = 0.9 μM (Hayakawa et al., 2020) and CHDs of other proteins, such as α-actinin (Kd = 4.7 μM; Wachsstock et al., 1993) or utrophin (Kd = 1.5 μM; Singh et al., 2017) do not show this behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research measuring binding affinities.

claim: CHDs of other proteins, such as α-actinin (Kd = 4.7 μM) or utrophin (Kd = 1.5 μM) do not show actin bending behavior.
source: The actin-binding affinity of Rng2(1-189) is Kd = 0.9 μM (Hayakawa et al., 2020) and CHDs of other proteins, such as α-actinin (Kd = 4.7 μM; Wachsstock et al., 1993) or utrophin (Kd = 1.5 μM; Singh et al., 2017) do not show this behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with other CHD-containing proteins and their cited binding affinities.

claim: Uyeda and colleagues reported that curly (Rng2(1-189)) in solution could induce kinks at random locations of the actin filament.
source: Recently, Uyeda and colleagues reported that curly (Rng2(1-189)) in solution could induce kinks at random locations of the actin filament (Hayakawa et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: One possibility for how curly induces actin bending when constrained to a lipid membrane could be asymmetric binding of curly to actin filaments leading to a succession of kinks towards the same direction.
source: We do not know yet the precise mechanism how curly induces actin bending when constrained to a lipid membrane, but one possibility could be asymmetric binding of curly to actin filaments leading to a succession of kinks towards the same direction.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism.

claim: With an estimated His6-Curly surface density on SLBs of 5000 µm−2, the approximated curly to actin ratio would be 1:7 or higher.
source: With an estimated His6-Curly surface density on SLBs of 5000 µm−2 (Nye and Groves, 2008) the approximated curly to actin ratio would be 1:7 or higher.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation using an estimated surface density from cited literature.

claim: The mobility of curly on the SLB allowing accumulation under actin filaments is essential for actin filament bending.
source: The mobility of curly on the SLB allowing accumulation under actin filaments is essential for actin filament bending as glass-immobilized curly failed to generate rings.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental comparison between mobile and immobilized curly.

claim: Studies of the Goode laboratory on IQGAP1 indicate that the N-terminal part IQGAP1(1–522), which corresponds to Rng2(1-189), is monomeric and does not promote bundling of actin filaments.
source: Studies of the Goode laboratory on IQGAP1 indicate that the N-terminal part IQGAP1(1–522), which corresponds to Rng2(1-189), is monomeric and does not promote bundling of actin filaments (Hoeprich et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The binding of curly to actin reduces the effective actin filament persistence length far below its typical value of 10 µm.
source: The binding of curly to actin reduces the effective actin filament persistence length far below its typical value of 10 µm.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed high curvatures of actin filaments.

claim: Addition of rabbit muscle myosin II filaments resulted in actin ring constriction without any evidence for filament breaking up to curvatures of 6.3 µm−1.
source: This increased flexibility is particularly highlighted by the fact that addition of rabbit muscle myosin II filaments resulted in actin ring constriction without any evidence for filament breaking up to curvatures of 6.3 µm−1 which is much higher than values reported for actin alone (C = 2.5 µm−1) (Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and comparison with literature values.

claim: The curvature of 6.3 µm−1 achieved with curly and myosin II is much higher than values reported for actin alone (C = 2.5 µm−1).
source: This increased flexibility is particularly highlighted by the fact that addition of rabbit muscle myosin II filaments resulted in actin ring constriction without any evidence for filament breaking up to curvatures of 6.3 µm−1 which is much higher than values reported for actin alone (C = 2.5 µm−1) (Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with literature values for actin curvature.

claim: It was not evident that the addition of myosin II filaments would lead to actin ring constriction without having to add any actin cross-linkers.
source: It was not evident that the addition of myosin II filaments would lead to actin ring constriction without having to add any actin cross-linkers.
evidence: The claim reflects the authors' expectation based on knowledge of typical requirements for ring constriction.

claim: A possible explanation for actin ring constriction is that the myosin II filament acts both as a cross-linker and motor protein, with one end at the actin filament plus end while other myosin head domains pull along the same actin filament toward the plus end leading to constriction.
source: When considering that curly arranges actin filaments into an inward spiral, a possible explanation for actin ring constriction would be that the myosin II filament acts both as a cross-linker and motor protein: one end of the myosin II filament sits at the actin filament plus end while other myosin head domains of the same myosin II filament pull along the same actin filament to travel toward the plus end leading to constriction.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the observed constriction mechanism.

claim: Sub-optimal myosin head orientations towards the actin filament could explain the observed slow constriction rates that were orders of magnitude slower than the reported values for actin propulsion by myosin II in motility assays.
source: This would result in sub-optimal myosin head orientations towards the actin filament, which could explain the observed slow constriction rates that were orders of magnitude slower than the reported values for actin propulsion by myosin II in motility assays (Toyoshima et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation based on comparison with literature values.

claim: Highly bent actin filament structures are most likely important for many cellular structures such as axons, mitochondrial actin cages, or secretion of the Weibel-Palade bodies.
source: Highly bent actin filament structures are most likely important for many cellular structures such as axons (Vassilopoulos et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2013), mitochondrial actin cages (Kruppa et al., 2018), or secretion of the Weibel-Palade bodies (Nightingale et al., 2011), but the molecular mechanisms leading to their formation are still poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to prior research and general knowledge of cellular structures.

claim: The molecular mechanisms leading to the formation of highly bent actin filament structures are still poorly understood.
source: Highly bent actin filament structures are most likely important for many cellular structures such as axons (Vassilopoulos et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2013), mitochondrial actin cages (Kruppa et al., 2018), or secretion of the Weibel-Palade bodies (Nightingale et al., 2011), but the molecular mechanisms leading to their formation are still poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the current state of the field.

claim: The system of membrane-bound curly, actin filaments, and myosin II filaments constitutes a minimalistic system for actin ring formation and constriction.
source: In addition, our system of membrane-bound curly, actin filaments, and myosin II filaments constitutes a minimalistic system for actin ring formation and constriction and could be used in the future to design synthetic dividing vesicles and further exiting active membrane-cortex systems.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental system and its potential applications.

claim: The system could be used in the future to design synthetic dividing vesicles and further exciting active membrane-cortex systems.
source: In addition, our system of membrane-bound curly, actin filaments, and myosin II filaments constitutes a minimalistic system for actin ring formation and constriction and could be used in the future to design synthetic dividing vesicles and further exiting active membrane-cortex systems.
evidence: The claim is speculative about future applications of the system.

claim: F-actin is semi-flexible with a persistence length of ~10 μm.
source: Although F-actin is semi-flexible with a persistence length of ~10 μm, binding of mobile curly within lipid membranes generates actin filament arcs and full rings of high curvature with radii below 1 μm.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about actin properties.

claim: Binding of mobile curly within lipid membranes generates actin filament arcs and full rings of high curvature with radii below 1 μm.
source: Although F-actin is semi-flexible with a persistence length of ~10 μm, binding of mobile curly within lipid membranes generates actin filament arcs and full rings of high curvature with radii below 1 μm.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Higher rates of fully formed actin rings are observed in the presence of the actin-binding coiled-coil protein tropomyosin.
source: Higher rates of fully formed actin rings are observed in the presence of the actin-binding coiled-coil protein tropomyosin and when actin is directly polymerized on lipid membranes decorated with curly.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing conditions with and without tropomyosin.

claim: Higher rates of fully formed actin rings are observed when actin is directly polymerized on lipid membranes decorated with curly.
source: Higher rates of fully formed actin rings are observed in the presence of the actin-binding coiled-coil protein tropomyosin and when actin is directly polymerized on lipid membranes decorated with curly.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing formin-driven polymerization versus landing of pre-formed filaments.

claim: Curly induced actin filament rings contract upon the addition of muscle myosin II filaments.
source: Strikingly, curly induced actin filament rings contract upon the addition of muscle myosin II filaments and expression of curly in mammalian cells leads to highly curved actin structures in the cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of ring contraction.

claim: Expression of curly in mammalian cells leads to highly curved actin structures in the cytoskeleton.
source: Strikingly, curly induced actin filament rings contract upon the addition of muscle myosin II filaments and expression of curly in mammalian cells leads to highly curved actin structures in the cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mammalian cell expression studies.

claim: Actin filaments are central to numerous biological processes in all domains of life.
source: Actin filaments are central to numerous biological processes in all domains of life.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton exhibits a variety of geometries driven by the interplay with molecular motors, actin binding and actin modulating proteins.
source: Driven by the interplay with molecular motors, actin binding and actin modulating proteins, the actin cytoskeleton exhibits a variety of geometries.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Structures with a curved geometry such as axon-stabilizing actin rings, actin cages around mitochondria and the cytokinetic actomyosin ring are generally assumed to be formed by short linear filaments held together by actin cross-linkers.
source: This includes structures with a curved geometry such as axon-stabilizing actin rings, actin cages around mitochondria and the cytokinetic actomyosin ring, which are generally assumed to be formed by short linear filaments held together by actin cross-linkers.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge and assumptions in the field.

claim: Whether individual actin filaments in curved structures could be curved and how they may assume a curved geometry remains unknown.
source: However, whether individual actin filaments in these structures could be curved and how they may assume a curved geometry remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of gaps in current understanding.

claim: Actin was purified from muscle acetone powder from rabbit.
source: Actin was purified from muscle acetone powder form rabbit (cat. no. M6890, Merck) and labeled with Alexa488-maleimide (cat. no. A10254, Thermo Fisher) following standard protocols (Pardee and Spudich, 1982).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used.

claim: Supported lipid bilayers containing 98% DOPC and 2% DGS-NTA(Ni2+) lipids were formed by fusion of small uni-lamellar vesicles.
source: Supported lipid bilayers (SLB) containing 98% DOPC (cat. no. 850375, Avanti Polar Lipids) and 2% DGS-NTA(Ni2+) (cat. no. 790404, Avanti Polar Lipids) lipids were formed by fusion of small uni-lamellar vesicles (SUV) that were prepared by lipid extrusion using a membrane with 100 nm pore size (cat. no. 610000, Avanti Polar Lipids).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used.

claim: HEK293T and RPE-1 cell lines were obtained from ATCC and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
source: We used the mammalian cell lines HEK293T and RPE-1 obtained from ATCC which were tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
evidence: The claim describes the cell lines used and their quality control.
